title: Micron did not need an endless memory boom
summary: BofA’s most useful Micron argument allowed memory prices to fall. The question was how much profit would remain.
watch: Whether contract protection and margins support the earnings BofA expected under lower memory prices.
tldr: BofA moved from a longer memory-cycle argument to a harder test: what Micron could earn if prices fell sharply.
Its August downside case still produced about $100 a share in earnings. That was a conditional forecast, not an established floor.
MU rose after the August 4 call, but Morgan Stanley also made a successful call nearby. The distinction was the question BofA asked, not exclusive foresight.
lead: A memory stock does not need prices to rise forever to be worth owning. It needs the price paid for the stock to make sense against the profits the business can retain when conditions weaken. That was the useful turn in BofA’s Micron research: by August 2026 it was willing to assume a downturn and still make a Buy case. The argument was more demanding than saying that AI would keep demand strong.
body: BofA had changed its view on December 18, 2025, upgrading Micron to Buy. The analyst reconsidered the durability of the memory cycle and the quality of the balance sheet. High-bandwidth memory was sold out through calendar 2026, and customers were entering multiyear agreements. BofA raised its fiscal 2026, 2027 and 2028 earnings estimates by 62%, 80% and 42%. Those were revisions to forecasts, not annual earnings growth rates.

The first chart window starts at the next trading day’s adjusted close, December 19. Over the following 20 trading sessions MU gained 46.39%, beating QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund, by 46.38 percentage points. The same next-session convention applies to every window here. The price supported the direction of the upgrade; it did not establish the long-term earnings case. Nor should the more detailed argument BofA made eight months later be credited to the December call.

On August 4, BofA accepted that memory pricing could normalize from mid-2027. Its base case put calendar 2028 earnings near $150 a share. Under a severe downturn, with average selling prices for DRAM and NAND falling 30% and 40%, it still modeled about $100. Earnings would fall by roughly a third between the two cases. This was not a claim that memory had stopped being cyclical. It was a claim that a weaker cycle could leave a different level of profit.

I find that distinction more useful than the price target. If the market is applying an old-cycle discount to a business with a different earnings base, a slowdown can be real and the discount can still be too large. BofA pointed to long-term agreements, the competitive position of high-bandwidth memory and continued AI infrastructure spending. Without the full cost model or the price sensitivities behind the $100 estimate, it is a testable scenario, not a guaranteed earnings floor or a floor under the share price.

MU rose 7.04% over the 20 sessions after the August 4 note, against a 1.12% fall in QQQ. That was a favorable price response. It was not uniquely BofA’s opportunity. Morgan Stanley also described the memory pullback as a tactical re-entry on August 7, arguing that longer contracts could improve visibility without eliminating cyclicality. MU gained 16.17% in the window following that note. The windows overlap heavily, so their difference cannot establish which analyst was better.

The later record also matters. BofA reiterated Buy on August 17 while discussing a longer-term valuation framework, but MU fell 1.51% over the next 20 sessions, slightly less than QQQ. I have not used the historical peak-earnings comparisons in the available summaries of the August notes: they quote incompatible figures whose definitions cannot be reconciled from that text. The useful part of the case survives without them.

BofA’s question differs from the ones Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo asked in the companion cases. Morgan Stanley separated a local efficiency improvement from the outlook for total memory demand. Wells Fargo separated Dell’s growth into orders, selling prices and the timing of several businesses. BofA asked whether a positive view could survive an unfavorable assumption. These are complementary research habits, not a ranking built from different stocks and dates.

What I would watch is the protection those agreements actually provide, the pace of price normalization and the margins Micron retains as the mix changes. A model that keeps $100 of earnings after a large price decline needs those mechanisms to hold. The stock’s earlier rise makes the call worth studying; the operating evidence will decide whether the earnings argument was right.

title: Better AI efficiency did not settle the memory question
summary: Morgan Stanley separated a local efficiency gain from total memory demand, then asked whether memory was a better way to own the AI opportunity.
watch: Whether aggregate demand, delivery premiums and supply constraints support memory pricing after efficiency improves.
tldr: Morgan Stanley argued that a reported improvement in the memory used by one inference component could not be applied to all memory demand.
It then preferred Micron and SanDisk as ways to express stronger AI-driven CPU demand, emphasizing supply constraints and pricing power.
MU rose 46.91% and 55.49% in the two 20-session windows. They overlap, and neither result proves that memory beat the CPU alternatives.
lead: An efficiency gain can be real while the market’s conclusion about it is too broad. In March 2026, Morgan Stanley applied that distinction to a sell-off in memory stocks around Google’s TurboQuant. A month later it took the argument beyond defending demand: if AI was making more computing necessary, which part of the supply chain offered the more attractive stock? Together, the two notes make a useful case in moving from a technical claim to an investment judgment.
body: On March 26, Morgan Stanley maintained Overweight on Micron and SanDisk. The firm argued that memory was becoming a constraint on AI demand, not simply a beneficiary of it. AI was absorbing DRAM supply that might otherwise go to PCs and smartphones, cloud customers were paying for expedited delivery, and the complexity of newer high-bandwidth memory would absorb additional capacity. These were specific reasons to question whether an efficiency improvement would quickly remove the shortage.

The disputed number needed a denominator. Morgan Stanley said the reported sixfold improvement applied to the key-value cache, the stored information an AI model uses while generating its response, rather than to all memory. A reduction in one component’s resource requirements cannot by itself establish a proportional reduction across workloads and memory types. I am describing the analyst’s interpretation of the technology, not independently verifying its benchmark.

That is the strongest part of the March call. It did not require denying the improvement or assuming that AI demand could never disappoint. It required checking what the improvement covered and whether it outweighed the other demands on supply. The next observations to examine were total demand, delivery conditions and pricing, not the headline efficiency multiple alone.

By April 20, Morgan Stanley was making a relative choice. It expected Intel and AMD to benefit from CPU demand associated with AI agents, but favored Micron and SanDisk as ways to express that demand. It raised its Intel target while retaining concerns about execution and market share. AMD had the stronger server position in its account, but a more balanced stock upside. Memory offered tighter supply, pricing power and a clearer path from additional AI demand to earnings.

The direct beneficiary of a trend is not necessarily the most attractive stock. Competition, available supply, the amount of profit retained and the price already paid for the shares all sit between a growing market and an investment return. Morgan Stanley’s April note made that distinction concrete. It was a comparison across several companies, not a newly verified upgrade of Micron on its own.

The chart shows MU and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund, from the first trading close after each note. From March 27 through April 27, MU rose 46.91%, against 18.07% for QQQ. From April 21 through May 19, it rose 55.49%, against 8.88%. Those are strong outcomes for the positive direction of the views. The windows overlap in late April, so the returns cannot be added or treated as two independent experiments. I have not compared Intel and AMD returns here, so this does not verify the full relative-stock recommendation.

These calls also change how I read the earlier institutional scorecard. They were absent from the structured event subset used for the ranking. A lower score for Morgan Stanley in that subset cannot erase them. Equally, adding just these successful observations to its hit rate would be selective. A revised ranking would need the same inclusion rules applied across institutions.

The research lesson is distinct from BofA’s later Micron downside case and Wells Fargo’s Dell work. BofA asked what earnings would survive lower prices; Wells Fargo traced the routes from demand to revenue. Morgan Stanley first checked whether the demand concern had been extended beyond the evidence, then compared where supply constraints could turn demand into profit. What I would watch next is whether those constraints persist as capacity arrives, whether delivery premiums fade and whether efficiency begins to change aggregate demand. A higher share price alone cannot answer those questions.

title: Dell’s AI upside had more than one route to revenue
summary: Wells Fargo looked beyond the AI server headline to orders, selling prices, conventional server replacements and a possible storage recovery.
watch: Whether orders convert into revenue and whether server replacements and storage improve on their own schedules.
tldr: Wells Fargo saw a path from Dell’s $50 billion AI server revenue target to a $60–65 billion upside scenario, supported by demand and selling prices.
It separately followed conventional server replacements and storage headwinds that could ease later. Those were different businesses and timing assumptions.
DELL rose 42.28% in the first 20-session window. The August follow-up initially lost money before recovering, and the longer-term revenue forecast remains unverified.
lead: AI spending was the headline in Dell’s story, but it was not a sufficient revenue model. Wells Fargo’s May 2026 argument was useful because it broke the opportunity into parts: orders from cloud customers, higher selling prices, replacements of conventional servers and a storage business with its own obstacles. The question was not simply whether AI spending would grow. It was which part of Dell could turn that spending into revenue, and when.
body: On May 22, Wells Fargo raised its Dell target from $180 to $270 and increased estimates for fiscal 2027 through 2029. The firm thought Dell’s $50 billion fiscal 2027 AI server revenue target was conservative. Stronger demand from cloud service providers and newer AI cloud operators, together with higher average selling prices, could support $60–65 billion. That was an analyst upside scenario, 20–30% above the company target, not an announced increase in company guidance or realized revenue.

The difference matters because it makes the positive view inspectable. A forecast above guidance needs additional orders, better delivery, higher prices or a different product mix. Wells Fargo named demand and pricing as drivers, but the available evidence does not show how much each contributes. That is enough to identify what needs checking, not enough to reproduce a complete financial model.

There were two other routes. Wells Fargo highlighted improving conventional server demand and faster Intel and AMD CPU replacement cycles. It also saw an underappreciated opportunity in AI-oriented storage as VMware VxRail headwinds eased in the second half of fiscal 2027. That storage argument combined new demand with a reduction in an existing obstacle. It should be followed separately from the large AI server orders rather than assumed to move on the same timetable.

In the August 14 follow-up, the firm retained Overweight and raised its target from $505 to $545. Conventional servers had become more prominent in the argument, supported by enterprise replacements and AI-agent demand. It saw fiscal 2027 AI server revenue potentially approaching $60 billion against roughly $56.5 billion modeled. Total remaining performance obligations were about $97 billion, up roughly 98% from a year earlier, while its fiscal 2027 and 2028 earnings forecasts rose 7% and 11%.

Those quantities are not interchangeable. Total remaining performance obligations are neither all AI server orders nor revenue already earned. The earnings changes are forecast revisions, not annual growth rates. And May’s $60–65 billion upside case and August’s figure near $60 billion do not establish a sequence of rising forecasts: the available summaries of the two notes use different comparison bases and leave out the research in between. What persists is the method of connecting business conditions to revenue, not a tidy line of ever-higher targets.

The chart starts each window at the first trading close after the note and compares adjusted closes with QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund. From May 26 through June 24, Dell gained 42.28% while QQQ fell 2.59%, a gap of 44.86 percentage points. Much of Dell’s move was already present after five sessions, when it was up 42.69%. The August call had a different path: down 9.72% after five sessions, then up 13.28% after 20, beating QQQ by 16.75 percentage points. A successful endpoint should not hide the early loss.

BofA had also argued in April that AI exposure across servers, storage and PCs supported stronger growth and a higher valuation. Dell rose strongly in the window after that note too. Wells Fargo did not uniquely discover the theme. Its distinctive contribution in the available evidence was a more explicit gap between company guidance and an upside case, alongside separate operating changes and dates for the other businesses. Neither the price gain nor that extra detail proves its revenue scenario has been realized.

I would read this alongside Morgan Stanley’s Micron demand argument and BofA’s Micron downside case. Morgan Stanley checked whether a technical efficiency claim justified a broad demand conclusion. Wells Fargo asked where demand would show up in the company’s sales. BofA asked what profit could remain if conditions worsened. These are useful questions in sequence, not permanent labels for the firms or a contest between different return windows. For Dell, the next checks are order conversion, selling prices and mix, the breadth of enterprise replacements, and whether storage improves when expected. Those results will tell us more than another target increase.

title: Software did not trade as one AI story
summary: AI hit nine software stocks together; by October they had split along what each company could show in its own results.
watch: Whether Salesforce pilots and delayed ServiceNow AI deals turn into paid production use.

chart.alt: Small-multiple price charts, one per company (CRM, TEAM, NOW, PLTR, CRWD, PANW, ZS, ADBE, INTU), each against QQQ and rebased to 100.

chartNote: Each panel shows one company against QQQ, adjusted close, rebased to 100 at Dec 31, 2025.
tldr: Nine software stocks fell together in early 2026 on fears that AI would shrink paid seats. By October they had split: CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks more than doubled for the year, while Adobe lost about a third and Intuit more than half.

The winners could show AI raising demand for what they already sell: seat growth at Atlassian, platform buying in security. Where AI was a new product to sell, as at Adobe and Salesforce, it was still around 2% of revenue.
The next test is conversion: whether pilots at Salesforce and AI interest at ServiceNow turn into paid use once cost, data quality and governance are dealt with.
lead: For the first half of 2026 the market traded software as a single bet against AI. The worry was simple: agents would cut the number of paid seats and let customers work around the applications they rent. All nine companies I followed fell in the first quarter, from −13% at Palo Alto Networks to −58% at Atlassian. By early October they had come apart, and the way they came apart says more than the sell-off did. The companies that could show AI raising demand for what they already sell recovered. The ones still waiting for AI to become a new line of revenue did not.
body: The chart sets each company against QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund, both at 100 at the end of 2025. Two security companies broke away: CrowdStrike finished up 130% and Palo Alto Networks up 119%, against 22% for QQQ. The third-quarter rebound was broad, with Atlassian up 131% in the quarter, Palantir 60%, Salesforce 47% and ServiceNow 35%, but it did not repair the first half. Through Oct 2 Salesforce was still down 11% for the year, ServiceNow 12% and Zscaler 13%. Atlassian (+16%) and Palantir (+6%) were positive and behind QQQ. Adobe was down 32% and Intuit 57%.

Analysts saw the split coming before the market priced it. In January Goldman Sachs rated Salesforce and ServiceNow Buy and Adobe Sell, arguing that value would collect in the software that coordinates AI agents across a company’s work. After that the calls went company by company. UBS downgraded ServiceNow in April after hearing no consistent customer commitment to it as that coordinating layer. A month later BofA rated ServiceNow Buy and Salesforce Underperform, noting that Agentforce brought in only about 2% of revenue. In security, JPMorgan argued in April that AI agents widen what attackers can reach and push customers toward large platforms, and Wells Fargo’s September checks with security chiefs pointed the same way. Morgan Stanley went the other way on Zscaler, downgrading it in April because its push beyond its core product had not caught on.

AI has helped where it made an existing product more necessary, and has not yet paid where it is a new product to sell. Atlassian is the cleanest example of the first. Its cloud growth sped up to 31% in August, and the whole cloud beat, about $49 million, came from more seats on Jira and Confluence and from bundles sold to existing customers, not from moving old customers to the cloud. That is the opposite of the seat-loss story the stock had been priced for. Security works the same way: more agents inside a company means more identities and devices to protect. After talking to Palo Alto Networks management in September, BTIG expected revenue growth above 17% next fiscal year against a consensus of 14.6%, with its AI security product rising from about $120 million of annual recurring revenue to more than $400 million. Adobe sits on the other side. Its AI-first products passed $650 million of annual recurring revenue in September, which sounds large until you see it is about 2.4% of the total, and new recurring revenue was slowing.

The constraint is not interest. It is turning interest into paid production use. The checks around Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference in September made that concrete. Oppenheimer’s customer survey found 85% had tested or deployed Agentforce, but nearly half were still in pilots. Jefferies heard that one large implementation partner saw success in only about 8% of deployments, and named pricing complexity, data readiness and decision fatigue as the hurdles. ServiceNow looked healthier on its core business: JPMorgan’s ten partner and customer conversations in early October found strong renewals and deal sizes up 10–20%. Yet the same checks found AI projects held up by the cost of running the models, data quality, governance and return-on-investment reviews, and partners described that demand as delayed rather than lost. The gap is not limited to these vendors. A BearingPoint study reported by Reuters on Oct 1 found only 13% of companies on track with their AI programs, even though nearly three-quarters reported positive financial results from them.

The worst performer has a problem AI does not fix. Intuit reset its guidance lower in August as it cut prices on its do-it-yourself tax product to win back customers. JPMorgan pointed out that online paying customers grew only 3% in fiscal 2026, down from 5%, while revenue per customer rose 15%. That is a customer-acquisition problem, not an AI one. Salesforce, down far less, has a milder version of it. Excluding its Informatica acquisition, organic growth was around 6.4–7%, and about 40% of the customers Oppenheimer surveyed keep their unified data outside Salesforce, which leaves room for data platforms or AI model companies to own the agent layer instead.

What I’m watching is conversion, company by company. At Salesforce, the share of Agentforce customers that move from pilots to paid use, and organic growth without acquisitions. At ServiceNow, whether the AI deals partners call delayed actually close. Atlassian starts usage billing on Dec 3, and Mizuho expects about 10% of cloud customers to face extra usage charges at first; that will be the first real price on its AI features. Palo Alto Networks has to turn BTIG’s forecast into its own guidance, Zscaler has a new head of sales to prove out, and Intuit needs customer additions to recover. A rebound in any of these stocks without those numbers would not tell me much.

sources.name: Atlassian, Adobe, Intuit, Palantir and Salesforce results

title: Meta’s AI products still need to earn their keep
summary: Meta’s ads are paying for AI; its new products have users but no revenue yet, against spending commitments that keep growing.
watch: Disclosed Muse revenue and a 2027 spending plan. Morgan Stanley expects little direct Muse revenue before late 2027.

chart.alt: Price chart of META against QQQ, rebased to 100, with numbered turning points: 1. Jul 28, 2025 Superintelligence Labs chief named; 2. Oct 29, 2025 Q3 guide lifts capex; 3. Jan 28, 2026 2026 capex guide; 4. Apr 8, 2026 Muse Spark released; 5. Apr 27, 2026 Manus unwind ordered; 6. Jul 30, 2026 Q2 results; 7. Sep 9, 2026 Muse adoption takes off.

chartNote: Meta against QQQ, adjusted close, rebased to 100 at Jun 26, 2025. Numbered markers are the turning points described in the text.
tldr: From June 2025 to October 2026 Meta’s stock rose 0.7% while the Nasdaq-100 rose 38%. Most big moves came on spending announcements (down) or new products (up).
AI is clearly paying off inside the ad business, where revenue grew 27% in the June quarter. Muse, the new consumer AI agent, has millions of users and no disclosed revenue.
My view: the real question is cost. Needham counts about $628 billion of lease and purchase commitments outside the usual valuation math, and Muse has to earn more than it costs to run.
lead: Meta is the clearest case of a market that believes in the product and doubts the bill. Over fifteen months the stock went almost nowhere while the Nasdaq-100 rose 38%, and nearly every large move in between came from one of two kinds of news. When Meta raised its spending plans, the shares fell. When it showed something people wanted to use, they jumped. The ad business underneath kept growing through all of it. What the market keeps arguing about is whether the spending around that business will earn its money back.
body: The chart sets Meta and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund, to 100 on Jun 26, 2025. The first big break came on Oct 30, 2025, the day after Meta raised its capital-spending guidance: the stock fell 11.3% while QQQ fell 1.5%. The next two spending updates went opposite ways, up 10.4% after January’s results and down 8.6% after April’s. July’s results, with ad growth but higher costs, took it down another 8.0% on a day QQQ rose 3.3%. By the end of April 2026 Meta was 15.5% below where the chart starts. Then Meta launched Muse, its consumer AI agent, on Sep 9, and the stock gained 21.4% in the next two weeks, including a 12% day on Sep 21. It still ended the period up only 0.7%, against 38.0% for QQQ.

Analysts mostly agreed on the ad business and disagreed on everything else. Piper Sandler credited Meta’s new ranking models with about a 7% yearly improvement in ad conversions as early as June 2025, and Morgan Stanley made Meta a top pick in March on forecasts of 28% and 21% ad growth for 2026 and 2027. BofA put the split plainly in June: the gains from better targeting were already visible, but the returns on Meta’s frontier-model spending were not. JPMorgan upgraded the stock after Muse launched, while still modeling $243 billion and $284 billion of capital spending in 2027 and 2028 and $65–70 billion a year of pressure on free cash flow. On the skeptical side, Needham argued in July that the spending was wearing down Meta’s return on capital. Morgan Stanley, still bullish, said on Oct 1 that it expects little direct revenue from Muse before late 2027 or 2028.

Whether AI makes Meta’s ads work better is largely settled. Ad revenue grew 27% in the June quarter excluding currency effects, and the company tied the gain to its models improving conversions. Piper’s third-party data had ad prices up 33% year on year in August, and an agency budget check in late September had Meta’s third-quarter ad spending growth speeding up to 13.5–14% from 12–12.5% three months earlier. The core business is paying its way.

Whether Muse becomes a business is not settled at all. The usage evidence is strong: No. 1 in the US App Store ten days after launch, and Sensor Tower data put it past 5.1 million US downloads in 22 days, more than twice ChatGPT’s 2.3 million over its first 22 days. Then the evidence turns. An Oppenheimer survey found 8% of consumers would trust Meta with their passwords, against 30% for Google. Amazon cut Muse off from shopping on Amazon.com within two weeks, objecting that it did not identify itself. MoffettNathanson estimated that only about 11 purchases a month per consumer are realistically something an agent could handle. Oppenheimer put the bar in numbers: lifting Meta’s earnings per share by 20% would take about $27.5 billion of agent revenue, roughly 115 million people paying $20 a month.

Whether the total investment earns an adequate return is where the market is right to be cautious, because the cost side is larger than the headline capital budget. In the June quarter adjusted operating margin fell about 6 percentage points, and free cash flow was about $0.8 billion on $60.8 billion of revenue. Needham counted roughly $628 billion of obligations that sit outside the usual valuation measure: about $278 billion of signed leases that have not started yet and $350 billion of commitments Meta cannot cancel. Including them raises Meta’s valuation multiple by about 35%, by Needham’s estimate, against roughly 9% for Amazon and 3% for Alphabet. Zuckerberg described the trade-off himself in May: compute and people are Meta’s two cost centers, and more of one means less of the other. Even the model side is contested. The Financial Times reported in June that Muse Spark, the rebuilt model behind Muse, reused Llama 4 code and data and still trails rivals at coding.

What I watch is the line that connects the product to the bill. In Meta’s next results: whether ad growth matches the 13.5–14% agency check; whether any Muse revenue is disclosed (Meta said at its Connect event that it plans to take a small fee on transactions, with Shopify, Walmart and Best Buy among the first connected merchants); and whether management finally gives a 2027 spending framework, which it declined to do in July. I would also track the commitments line, since Meta signed about $68 billion more in leases in July alone. Usage growth without those numbers keeps Muse a popularity story.

sources.name: Sensor Tower data via Wells Fargo and others

title: Optical demand is strong; future profits face harder tests
summary: Laser scarcity has shown up in Lumentum’s margins; the bigger bets on packaging and trade policy are still forecasts.
watch: Whether laser prices and margins hold as capacity grows, and any adopted import rule that names products.

chart.alt: Price chart of LITE, COHR against QQQ, rebased to 100, with numbered turning points: 1. Oct 13, 2025 Aletheia initiates on scarcity; 2. Jan 20, 2026 Rebuttal on wafer supply; 3. Apr 9, 2026 JPM raises post-OFC forecasts; 4. Jun 10, 2026 Interim optical designs defended; 5. Aug 11, 2026 LITE reports upside; 6. Sep 24, 2026 PhotonLink value questioned; 7. Oct 1, 2026 Analysts question policy gains.

chartNote: Lumentum and Coherent against QQQ, adjusted close, rebased to 100 at Oct 10, 2025. Numbered markers are turning points.
tldr: In a year Lumentum rose 626% and Coherent 203%, against 28% for the Nasdaq-100, on one idea: the lasers that carry AI data traffic are scarce.
That idea has held up in results. Lumentum beat on margins in August and guided revenue about 8% above forecasts, and both companies say supply, not demand, is the limit.
I keep it separate from the bets stacked on top (the timing of new optics packaging, Coherent’s platform push, US import limits), which are mostly forecasts and drove the sharpest swings.
lead: The optical story has two layers, and they have behaved very differently. The bottom layer is a simple claim: the lasers that move data between AI chips are in short supply, so the few companies that make them can raise prices. That claim kept being confirmed. Stacked on top were bigger claims about new ways of packaging optics, new markets and help from trade policy. Those were priced in quickly and then questioned, and they account for most of the sharp swings in the stocks.
body: The chart sets Lumentum, Coherent and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund, to 100 on Oct 10, 2025. Through Oct 2, 2026 Lumentum rose 626% and Coherent 203%, against 28% for QQQ. Most of that came early: by late May Lumentum was up about 500% and Coherent about 240%. Then the group stalled. From late May to early August Lumentum fell 14% and Coherent 24%, and by mid-June Lumentum had been roughly flat since April while chip stocks broadly rallied. August brought the sharpest back-and-forth. Both stocks rose on Aug 4 on a report of possible US limits on Chinese optical parts, fell 10–14% six days later when that report was narrowed, and then Lumentum’s results restarted the climb. From Aug 10 to Sep 23 Lumentum gained 15% while Coherent lost 8%.

Brokers built the case from scarcity up. Aletheia started coverage in October 2025 forecasting that Lumentum’s earnings per share would roughly quadruple between fiscal 2025 and 2028. In April, after the industry’s main trade show, JPMorgan raised its Lumentum target to $950 and sketched 2028 revenue near $10 billion. It also lifted its estimate of the market for co-packaged optics, where the optical parts sit in the same package as the chip, to more than $15 billion from $5 billion. Lumentum’s chief executive told Bloomberg the company expected to be sold out through 2028 within two quarters. The skeptics went after timing rather than demand. UBS expected optics inside computing racks to arrive closer to 2029. SemiAnalysis argued in June that volume production of co-packaged optics would start in 2029, not 2028. A Taiwanese trade report in September put the larger ramp in 2028–29.

The scarcity claim is the one with real evidence, because it shows up in reported margins and in what both suppliers and customers say. Lumentum’s June quarter, reported in August, beat on revenue ($1.006 billion against $990 million expected), on gross margin (50.4% against 48.8%) and on earnings. Its guidance for the next quarter was about 8% above analyst revenue forecasts and 16% above on earnings. Coherent’s management said at a JPMorgan event in late September that supply, not demand, is the limit. Stifel, after meeting Lumentum’s chief executive at the ECOC conference, reported that the company could not fully meet December-quarter demand for the lasers used in Nvidia’s systems. Mizuho said in September that indium phosphide wafers, the material these lasers are built on, remain the binding constraint, and that real relief from larger wafers is unlikely before 2028.

The packaging debate matters less for laser makers than the stock moves implied. When SemiAnalysis pushed back the co-packaged timeline, Lumentum fell 8% in a day and won back about half of it the next. But the main alternative, near-packaged optics, where the optical parts sit next to the chip rather than inside its package, still needs the same lasers. AMD said in September that its 2027 accelerator will run copper and near-packaged optics side by side, and both Citi and Bernstein argued Lumentum keeps similar laser economics either way. Where the design choice does matter is in who captures the value of the full system. That is Coherent’s bet with its PhotonLink platform, and it is where the evidence is weakest. Some investors read PhotonLink as a bundling of existing products rather than a new business, and Bernstein expects Coherent to get less margin lift than Lumentum because it makes more of its own components. That fits Coherent lagging Lumentum after August.

The policy upside is the thinnest leg. The August report of a possible US ban on Chinese optical transceivers sent Coherent up 12% and Lumentum up 9%. Within a week CLSA found that the draft rule did not target any of the ten largest transceiver makers, and the stocks gave the gains back. B. Riley called the draft a bargaining chip and noted that China controls about 70% of refined indium production. A Reuters report in late September cited research saying Coherent and Lumentum lack the scale to replace Chinese suppliers. On Oct 1 Morgan Stanley’s strategists suggested any rule would start with China-made 3.2-terabit modules and leave today’s 800-gigabit and 1.6-terabit products alone, which, as one investor pointed out, barely touches Chinese module makers in the near term.

The risk I would put first is new supply. Rosenblatt expects indium phosphide laser capacity to grow about twelvefold from 2025 to 2030, Mizuho has flagged worries about too much capacity being added worldwide, and competitors such as Source Photonics have been ramping their own lasers faster than expected. Scarcity pricing lasts only as long as demand outruns that build. So I would watch Lumentum’s next quarter against its $1.25 billion revenue guide and whether gross margin holds above 50%; Coherent’s margins on their own rather than as a read-across from Lumentum; whether laser prices keep rising, as Citi expects with another 15% increase early in 2027; and, for policy, only an adopted rule that names products and dates.

title: Reddit’s ads are growing faster than its audience
summary: Reddit’s ads grew fast while its US audience, still dependent on Google, stopped growing.
watch: Reported daily users against weak third-party tracking, and a signed Google licensing renewal.

chart.alt: Price chart of RDDT against QQQ, rebased to 100, with numbered turning points: 1. Jul 28, 2025 DAU growth stabilizes; 2. Oct 9, 2025 ChatGPT citation risk; 3. Apr 2, 2026 Licensing pitched as engine; 4. May 1, 2026 Q1: ads strong, users flat; 5. Jul 31, 2026 Ads grow; fewer US users; 6. Sep 16, 2026 App versus search divergence; 7. Oct 2, 2026 Latest traffic and downloads.

chartNote: Reddit against QQQ, adjusted close, rebased to 100 at Jul 25, 2025. Numbered markers are turning points.
tldr: Reddit’s ad revenue grew 74% and then 64% in the first two quarters of 2026, yet the stock ended about flat (−1%) while the Nasdaq-100 rose 33%.
The reason is the audience: US daily users fell in the June quarter as Google sent fewer visitors, and Reddit stopped reporting the logged-in figures that showed loyal use.
App growth and a larger Google licensing deal could fix that, but neither is in reported results yet, so I treat the ad strength as necessary but not enough.
lead: Reddit is earning more from each visitor while becoming less sure how many visitors it will have. Through 2026 its advertising grew faster than almost anyone’s in online ads, and the stock still finished about where it started. The audience those ads are sold against depends heavily on Google, and on AI chatbots that may or may not send people back.
body: The chart sets Reddit and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund, to 100 on Jul 25, 2025. Over the full period Reddit fell 1.2% while QQQ rose 33.1%. Earnings days set the path. On May 1, first-quarter results with ad revenue up 74% sent the stock up 14%, and it gained 21% from the end of April to the end of July. On Jul 31, second-quarter results beat again on revenue, but US daily users fell and the stock dropped 14%. Being added to the S&P 500 gave it an 11% lift in mid-August that faded. From the July report to mid-September it was down about 9%, and it slipped further as third-party tracking turned weaker.

Analysts have been bullish on the ad engine and divided on the audience. Jefferies’ checks in July 2025 pointed to performance ads and small-business demand lifting revenue per user. RBC’s small-business checks in January were weaker, describing low prices and uneven conversions. In April Needham made Reddit a top pick on the idea that it is becoming a human-verified source for AI, cited in more than 35% of AI answers, and estimated that its roughly $60 million a year from each of OpenAI and Google could double. Wells Fargo in September estimated a new Google deal could be worth $250–300 million a year from 2027, while arguing that Google’s new payments to publishers lower the odds of favorable terms.

The advertising improvement is real and not much in dispute. In the March quarter revenue was $663 million, up 69%, and ad revenue $625 million, up 74%, with more than 60% coming from performance ads that advertisers buy for measurable results. Reddit’s automated campaign product delivered 17% lower cost per sale and 25% more conversions on average, and the number of active advertisers grew more than 75%. In the June quarter revenue was $805 million against about $730 million expected, ad revenue rose 64% and revenue per user 36%. A new Shopify integration that lets merchants load their catalogs directly widens that funnel further.

The audience depends on products Reddit does not control. In the June quarter US daily users were 53.2 million, up 6% from a year earlier but down 0.3 million from the quarter before, and both logged-in and logged-out users fell. Reddit said it would stop reporting that split, which removes the clearest measure of whether it is replacing search visitors with regular users just as that became the main question. The outside data mostly points the wrong way. Google search traffic to Reddit fell 5.9% year on year in the third quarter after rising 8.9% in the second, according to Similarweb figures cited by Guggenheim. One tracker counted Reddit’s share of ChatGPT search citations falling from 3.8% to 0.5% over a few weeks in August. And in May Google’s AI search began showing “perspectives” from forums like Reddit inside its answers, which can keep users on Google. As one investor put it in April, it is hard to think of a mid-sized internet company that worked once its user base stalled.

The fixes are plausible and not yet in the reported numbers. Guggenheim’s data showed app downloads up 47% year on year and app daily users up 38%, and the chief executive said new-user retention rose 50% last quarter. Downloads are not retention, though, and the same executive conceded that Reddit’s recommendation feed is a year to 18 months behind the best in the industry. Piper Sandler’s data showed August users up 18% year on year, but Piper also flagged a change in measurement method expected to reset the reported audience size by about 20%, so that comparison is hard to lean on. On licensing, talks with Google are active but nothing is signed, and the current deals are small next to revenue running above $800 million a quarter.

The near-term test is the next results report. Yipit’s tracking had US and international daily users heading for misses of about 1.5 million and 4.5 million; a beat would challenge that read and a miss would confirm it. I would read the user number against the change in measurement, look for any disclosure of app or logged-in use, and watch for a signed Google renewal, which RBC expects in early 2027. Until users stabilize, strong ad growth is necessary but not enough.

sources.name: Reddit CEO at Goldman Sachs conference

title: AI spending: four companies, different paths to payback
summary: Four companies, one AI build-out, and very different amounts of cash left after paying for it.
watch: Operating cash minus capital spending, and new lease commitments, in the September-quarter reports.

chart.alt: Small-multiple price charts, one per company (GOOGL, MSFT, AMZN, META), each against QQQ and rebased to 100.

chartNote: Each panel shows one company against QQQ, adjusted close, rebased to 100 at Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta all trailed the Nasdaq-100 from January to October 2026, even as their cloud businesses grew 37–82%.
Their cash positions are far apart. In the June quarter Microsoft had about $20 billion of operating cash left after capital spending; Alphabet and Amazon spent more than they brought in.
My view: Microsoft’s cash and Amazon’s pricing power are the strongest evidence. Alphabet’s payback is still a management claim, and Meta’s depends on revenue it hasn’t reported yet.
lead: By the middle of 2026 the question about the four largest AI spenders had moved from whether demand was real to whether the spending turns into cash. Their cloud and ad businesses grew quickly all year, and all four still lagged the Nasdaq-100. Put their June-quarter filings side by side and part of the reason is plain: they are spending at very different rates relative to what their businesses bring in, and growth alone has not been enough to win the market over.
body: Each panel sets one company and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund, to 100 on Jan 22, 2026. Through Oct 2 QQQ rose 21.2%. Microsoft rose 15.4%, Meta 12.7%, Amazon 7.3% and Alphabet 4.1%, so all four trailed. Each had a deep fall along the way: Meta dropped 29% from late January to late March, Microsoft 26% from late January to late June, Alphabet 21% from mid-May to late July and Amazon 19% in the first weeks of February. The low point in sentiment came in June, when free cash flow, returns and the chance of share sales to fund the build-out were the main worries. July’s results, with faster cloud growth and much more talk about return on investment, started the recovery for Microsoft and Amazon.

Early in the year analysts mostly raised forecasts. Wolfe lifted its 2026 growth estimates for Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud in January, and TD Cowen argued in March that Amazon’s revenue per dollar of capital spending would recover toward historical levels by 2028. By late May the tone had changed: the companies themselves were saying capital spending was rising mainly because components cost more, not because they were adding that much more computing. In the fall the checks split by company. Citi saw Google’s new Gemini model improving its product prospects at low introductory prices. Wells Fargo expected Microsoft’s Azure growth to beat guidance but left its margin and cash-flow estimates almost unchanged, and reported Amazon raising its prices for reserved chip capacity again. Morgan Stanley expected little direct revenue from Meta’s new Muse agent until late 2027, and Needham argued Meta’s off-balance-sheet commitments make it much more expensive than standard measures show.

The cash positions are far apart. In the June quarter Microsoft generated $55.4 billion of operating cash and spent $35.8 billion on property and equipment, leaving about $20 billion. Meta was roughly even, with $31.9 billion in and $30.1 billion out. Alphabet spent about $6 billion more than its operating cash flow, and Amazon about $9 billion more. These are company-wide numbers, not returns on AI specifically, but they show who is paying for the build-out from current business and who is not. Growth rates do not sort them the same way. Google Cloud grew 82% with a 36% operating margin. Amazon Web Services grew 37% with a 39% margin, a figure that includes $0.6 billion of non-cash gains on energy contracts. Azure grew 43%, and Microsoft does not disclose its profit.

Pricing shows who has the stronger hand with customers. Amazon raised its prices for reserved GPU capacity for the fourth quarter in a row in October, by 15% on top of 20% in July, for a total increase of about 40–75% this year depending on the chip. That says demand is still ahead of supply, though contracted capacity means the revenue arrives with a lag. Microsoft, by contrast, is paying for some of its growth: Wells Fargo’s checks found it discounting Copilot seats to secure customers’ commitments to spend on Azure. Google is using price to win share. Citi noted that its new model’s introductory price of $2 per million input tokens is well below the roughly $10 frontier competitors charge.

More spending is not the same as more capacity, and financing is starting to blur the cost. If component inflation drives much of the rise in capital spending, each dollar buys less computing, which pushes payback further out; third-party checks in September also showed Amazon’s and Microsoft’s capacity growth slowing from August. Meanwhile some of the cost is moving onto other lines. The Financial Times reported Amazon in talks to sell about $8 billion of already-installed Nvidia chips to an outside-funded vehicle and lease them back, as it heads toward about $220 billion of capital spending this year. Needham counted roughly $628 billion of Meta obligations that standard valuation leaves out. Microsoft’s apparent cut to its 2026 spending figure in July turned out to be mostly an accounting reclassification. Google Cloud’s chief executive says AI servers pay for themselves in under two years, but that is management’s estimate, not something the filings show.

So when these companies report the September quarter, I would look past cloud growth to three things: operating cash flow minus capital spending, new lease and purchase commitments, and whether Amazon’s price increases show up in revenue. Until the companies disclose revenue and profit tied to their AI investments, I don’t think there is a defensible single winner on AI returns, only different amounts of evidence. Today Microsoft’s cash and Amazon’s pricing are the strongest. Alphabet’s product momentum is promising but its payback is still a claim. Meta’s case rests most on revenue it has not yet reported.

title: Memory and storage: one AI cycle, four different businesses
summary: Four memory makers rose and fell together in 2026; high-bandwidth memory share, contracts and new supply are what separate them.
watch: Whether price increases keep slowing after about +20% in the third quarter, and who wins HBM4 share at Nvidia.

chart.alt: Small-multiple price charts for SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron and SanDisk, each against QQQ and rebased to 100 at Dec 31, 2025 on a shared log scale, with the late-June to July 30 sell-off shaded.

chartNote: Each panel shows one company against QQQ, adjusted close, rebased to 100 at Dec 31, 2025, on a shared log scale. SK Hynix and Samsung are in won, QQQ in dollars, so “vs QQQ” is the gap between local-currency returns, not a dollar-adjusted excess return. Shaded: the late-June to July 30 sell-off.
tldr: Through Oct 2, SK Hynix, Samsung, Micron and SanDisk were up 131% to 625% for the year, and along the way each fell 39–56% from its late-June high to its low on Jul 29 or 30, even though memory prices kept rising.

The market trades them as one AI memory bet, but they sell different things: high-bandwidth memory for AI chips, ordinary server and phone memory, and flash storage, each with its own supply and customers.

My view: scarcity is real across all of them for now. What separates them is high-bandwidth memory share (Samsung is gaining on SK Hynix), how much is under contract, and how much new supply each faces by 2028.
lead: In 2026 the market treated memory as one AI trade. The four largest listed makers I follow rose together, fell together in July and recovered together, and on the worst days the moves were nearly identical. But they are not one business. AI raises demand at several levels at once: DRAM, the working memory in servers and phones; HBM, the stacked high-bandwidth DRAM that sits beside AI chips; NAND flash, used in solid-state drives; and hard drives for bulk storage. SK Hynix is mostly DRAM and HBM, with a flash business that includes Solidigm. Samsung makes DRAM, HBM and NAND flash. Micron makes the same three. SanDisk makes only flash. None of the four makes hard drives. The shared rally hid real differences in who sells what, and those differences started to show in the second half of the year.
body: The chart sets each company and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund, to 100 at the end of 2025, on a log scale so that a doubling looks the same in every panel. Through Oct 2 SanDisk was up 625%, Micron 277%, SK Hynix 183% and Samsung 131% (the Korean shares in won), against 22% for QQQ. All four peaked in late June and hit their lows on Jul 29 or 30: SanDisk fell 56%, SK Hynix 55%, Samsung 43% and Micron 39%. Three days did most of the damage. On Jul 7 Samsung’s preliminary results beat by less than investors had hoped; on Jul 13 Korea’s market fell 9%, taking SK Hynix down 15% and Samsung 11%; and on Jul 28, one of Korea’s worst sessions on record, the four fell between 9% and 15%. The rebound was uneven. From Jun 30 to Oct 2 Micron was down 7%, Samsung 17%, SanDisk 24% and SK Hynix 31%, while QQQ was up 2%.

The July drop came with almost no bad news on prices, which is why I read it as positioning more than fundamentals. Samsung’s July results still showed DRAM and flash prices rising strongly, and industry checks in late August had third-quarter memory prices finishing about 20% higher. What changed was who was holding the stocks. Situational Awareness, a hedge fund with large memory positions, was reported on Jul 30 to have sold its public portfolio to Citadel after heavy losses; that day Micron rose 18% and SanDisk 26%, and by Aug 4 markets were back where they had been before the unwind began.

Analysts mostly agreed on demand and argued about how long it lasts. JPMorgan, starting coverage of SK Hynix in September, called the cycle mid-stage, with more than half of SK Hynix’s capacity under long-term agreements and earnings per share growing about 34% a year through 2027. UBS raised its third-quarter DRAM price forecast to +23%, above the roughly 18% consensus. Evercore argued that AI agents, which keep their working state in memory, raise demand across every tier at once. Bernstein took the longer view: shortages of ordinary memory through 2027, then more capacity and limits on AI budgets bringing prices down in 2028, with supplier gross margins falling from around 90% at the peak toward the high 70s. Through September the bears’ main worries were that price increases were slowing and that Chinese supply was coming.

High-bandwidth memory is what divides the suppliers, and the share is moving. Bernstein’s tracking of Korean exports in July implied Samsung’s HBM revenue could rise about 80% in the third quarter while SK Hynix’s fell about 20%, which it put down to delayed shipments of the newest generation, HBM4, for Nvidia’s Rubin chips rather than weaker demand. Samsung’s HBM4 yields were reported to have climbed to about 80% from 60% at the start of production, it expected third-quarter HBM4 revenue to more than triple, and on Oct 2 it was reported to be asking mid-to-high $4 per gigabit for HBM4 in 2027, against about $1.50 for the previous generation. Micron said most of its 2027 HBM supply is already contracted at significantly higher prices and that it is co-developing a custom HBM4E with Nvidia. That shift fits the chart: SK Hynix, which had led the HBM market, had the weakest second half of the four. It also cuts both ways for the group. Bernstein trimmed its 2027 HBM price forecast because more competition means HBM may end up less profitable than ordinary DRAM.

The scarcity is broad right now because HBM eats capacity. HBM needs more than three times the wafer capacity of ordinary DRAM for the same number of bits, and Samsung expects it to take nearly 30% of the industry’s DRAM wafers in 2027, up from about 20%. That squeezes the ordinary memory everyone else buys. Micron’s results on Oct 1 showed it clearly: flash prices rose about 30% in the quarter against about 20% expected, and flash drove two-thirds of the revenue beat. So the flash-heavy names are not riding on someone else’s AI story; they are getting the overflow. The limit is the customer. Kioxia’s chief executive told his sales team in September not to push steep price increases on data-center buyers because their budgets are finite, Micron flagged that PC and smartphone unit sales could fall by double digits in 2026, and fourth-quarter price increases were tracking 5–10%, well below the third quarter’s.

Contracts and buybacks change the shape of this cycle. New supply is coming, and it lands unevenly. More of each company’s output is now committed: over half of SK Hynix’s capacity, according to JPMorgan; more than 75% of Micron’s 2027 output, with long-term agreements covering over 35% of its expected revenue through 2030, most of them with price ceilings as well as floors; and half of SanDisk’s flash this fiscal year, rising to two-thirds in fiscal 2028, at about 80% gross margin at the price floor. The companies are also handing cash back: SK Hynix announced a new buyback in August and committed to return more than half of its 2025–27 free cash flow, and SanDisk put $4.5 billion of a $5 billion quarter of free cash flow into buybacks. The supply side differs by company and product. SK Hynix is expanding its flash plant in Dalian by about 50%, and talks reported in September about making memory with Intel in the US by 2030 knocked the whole group down. Micron’s capital spending will rise more than 80% next fiscal year, mostly on clean rooms usable from late 2028. In China, CXMT, which listed in Shanghai in July, reached 10% of global DRAM in the June quarter, and YMTC is preparing a roughly $5 billion listing with the aim of leading the flash market by the end of 2027.

So I would stop asking whether memory is in a good cycle and ask which part of it each company sells. For the October reports I would watch the pace of price increases after the third quarter’s roughly 20%; who wins HBM4 volume at Nvidia, and whether SK Hynix catches up later this year as Bernstein expects; whether customers accept Samsung’s HBM4 premium; how much of each company’s output sits under contracts with price floors; and every new supply announcement, from CXMT’s high-bandwidth memory qualification to YMTC’s listing and any SK Hynix plant in the US. Shared demand does not mean equal returns.

sources.name: Samsung and SK Hynix statements as reported

title: One session, two ad-tech results, two separate questions
summary: Same day, same AI advertising label: AppLovin was graded on a broken pattern, Unity on confirmed checks.
watch: AppLovin’s new e-commerce advertiser counts, and a second quarter of Vector growth at Unity.

chart.alt: Bar chart of one-session returns for APP, U and QQQ.

chartNote: One-session returns, Aug 5 to Aug 6, 2026 close, for AppLovin, Unity and QQQ.
tldr: When both reported on Aug 6, 2026, AppLovin fell 20% and Unity rose 15% in one session, while the Nasdaq-100 slipped 0.4%.
AppLovin still grew revenue 53%, but it missed estimates for the first time since 2022 and switched its e-commerce plan from self-serve sign-ups to slower, partner-led sales.
Unity’s ad business beat because its new targeting engine, Vector, kept taking share, as checks had shown. My view: these were two separate tests, each graded against the company’s own record.
lead: On Aug 6, 2026, the two companies most tied to AI-driven mobile advertising reported on the same morning and went in opposite directions. AppLovin fell about 20% and Unity rose about 15%, while the market barely moved. It is tempting to read that as one AI advertising theme with a winner and a loser. I think it was two separate tests, and each company was graded against its own track record.
body: The chart shows one session, from the close on Aug 5 to the close on Aug 6. AppLovin returned −19.7%, Unity +15.1% and QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 fund, −0.4%, so AppLovin trailed the market by about 19 percentage points and Unity beat it by about 15. A single session cannot separate the advertising news from everything else in each report, so I treat the bars as the market’s verdict on the day, not as a measure of what advertising alone was worth.

The checks before the reports pointed different ways. In July BofA cut its forecasts for how many e-commerce advertisers AppLovin would sign up, while Morgan Stanley had expected self-serve sign-ups to add 200–300 non-gaming advertisers a month. For Unity, Wells Fargo raised its estimate for Vector, Unity’s rebuilt ad-targeting engine, to 15% growth over the prior quarter, and a Jefferies survey of mobile-game advertisers found Unity gaining about 2 percentage points of spending share, largely from AppLovin and smaller networks.

AppLovin was punished for breaking a pattern more than for slowing down. Revenue was $1.924 billion, up 53% from a year earlier, with a profit margin before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of 84%. Few companies anywhere grow like that. But revenue fell short of the $1.942 billion consensus and landed near the bottom of guidance. It was AppLovin’s first miss since 2022, after 12 to 14 quarters of beating the top of its range by about 5.5% on average, and the model upgrade investors expected had not arrived in the quarter. For a stock priced on steady self-learning gains, an in-range quarter was a bigger signal than the growth rate.

AppLovin also changed how it plans to grow e-commerce, and the number it offered in support measured something different. Instead of broad self-serve sign-ups, it will rely on partners to bring in mid-sized advertisers, which is slower. The 28% figure in the report compared consumer advertisers’ spending with their previous holiday peak; it measures spending on the platform, not AppLovin’s revenue. BofA downgraded the stock five days later and cut its 2027 growth estimate to 23% from 31%. The bull case was still coherent. Third-quarter guidance implied about 7.6% growth over the second quarter, above the usual 3–5% for the season, and RBC said after meeting management that a model upgrade had been held back for the third quarter on purpose. Both of those are promises, though, and the miss was a reported number.

Unity rose because the checks were confirmed, not because of a surprise. Its advertising business, Grow Solutions, brought in $389 million, up 35%. The figure investors watched was Strategic Grow, which leaves out the ad network and other businesses Unity is winding down: $329 million, up 63% year on year against about $306 million expected. Vector grew more than 20% in the quarter, above expectations in the high teens. Total revenue was $546 million and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization were $160 million, 18% above forecasts. HSBC, BofA and Deutsche Bank all upgraded the stock the next day. The rest of Unity was quieter. Its game-engine business, Create Solutions, grew 2% as reported; the strategic part of it grew 5%, or 14% once a $12 million one-time item from a year earlier is excluded, and roughly met forecasts. This was an advertising quarter, not a whole-company one.

From that day, the things worth following were simple. For AppLovin, whether partners actually bring in advertisers (monthly counts of new e-commerce advertisers would ease the execution question in a way partner announcements cannot) and whether the promised model upgrade shows up in third-quarter revenue. For Unity, whether Vector keeps growing for another quarter with its revenue contribution stated, since one beat cannot show the gains will last. Shared exposure to AI advertising told you little that day. Each company’s own operating numbers told you most of what mattered.
